explanation: I has continuous partial derivative −2txe^(−t²x) for all real t. III has continuous partial derivative −2t/(x²+t²)² on every local rectangle with c>0. II fails the stated theorem because the t derivative of |x−t| does not exist at x=t for 0<t<1. Therefore, the theorem applies throughout the stated domains only for I and III.

source_feedback_interpretation.source_problem:
For which of the following functions is it valid to differentiate under the integral sign?

- ${F}_{1}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{-{t}^{2}x}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in R$
- ${F}_{2}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}|x-t|\,\text{d}x,\,t\ge 0$
- ${F}_{3}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}x,\,t>0$
source_feedback_interpretation.interpreted_problem:
For which of the following functions does the continuous-partial-derivative sufficient theorem apply throughout the stated parameter domain? Apply the theorem locally on a rectangle $[0,1]\times[c,d]$: the integrand and its partial derivative with respect to $t$ must both be continuous there, and the partial derivative must exist at every point of the rectangle.

- ${F}_{1}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{-{t}^{2}x}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in R$
- ${F}_{2}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}|x-t|\,\text{d}x,\,t\ge 0$
- ${F}_{3}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}x,\,t>0$
source_feedback_interpretation.confidence_scope: Applicability of the explicitly stated sufficient theorem only. II admits differentiation by dominated convergence; failure of this theorem does not forbid interchange.
